title: Tips to Make Out: How to Kiss With Confidence and Chemistry
h1: Tips to Make Out: How to Kiss With Confidence, Chemistry and Consent
description: Nervous about your next kiss? These tips to make out cover consent, pacing, technique, keeping it fresh and building confidence so it feels great for both.
excerpt: Great make-outs come from slowing down, reading each other and keeping it fun. Here's how to kiss with confidence and real chemistry.
intro:
Making out should feel exciting, not like a test. Yet plenty of people, whether it is their first kiss or their hundredth, worry about where their hands go, what to do with their tongue or whether they are “doing it right.” The truth is that great kissing is less about technique and more about attention: paying attention to the other person, to the pace and to what feels good for both of you.

These tips to make out walk you through consent, setting the mood, starting slow, keeping things interesting and building confidence. Use what fits, skip what does not and remember that a little awkwardness is part of the fun.
body:
Start with consent and comfort

The best make-out sessions start with two people who both want to be there. Consent is not a one-time checkbox; it is an ongoing, mutual “yes.” Look for clear signals: they lean in, kiss back, pull you closer, keep eye contact. If they hesitate, turn away or go still, pause and check in.

Asking does not ruin the moment. It often makes it better. Try a soft “Can I kiss you?” or, once you are already kissing, “Is this okay?” or “Do you like that?” Those questions show confidence and care, which are both attractive.

Tip: Alcohol and kissing often go together, but if someone is too drunk to clearly communicate, they cannot give real consent. Save it for another night when you are both clear-headed.

Set the mood before the first kiss

  • Fresh breath: Brush, floss or keep mints or gum handy. Lip balm helps with dry lips.
  • A comfortable setting: A couch, a quiet corner or a parked car (with the engine off) beats a crowded hallway.
  • Build closeness first: Sit near each other, hold hands, let conversation get a little flirty. Kisses feel more natural when there is already warmth.
  • Put the phone away: Nothing kills the mood like a buzzing notification.

If you are working up to a first kiss with someone new, our guide on how to get a girl to kiss you covers reading the moment.

Slow and steady: how to begin

Rushing is the most common make-out mistake. Starting slow builds anticipation and gives you both time to find a rhythm.

  1. Begin with soft, closed-mouth kisses. Gentle and unhurried. Let the kiss linger for a second or two.
  2. Tilt your head slightly. It keeps noses from bumping and feels more natural.
  3. Relax your lips. Tense, puckered lips feel stiff. Soft and slightly parted is ideal.
  4. Follow their lead, then trade. Kissing is a conversation. Mirror their pace, then take turns leading.
  5. Ease into deeper kissing. If you both want to, slightly part your lips and introduce your tongue gently and briefly. Less is more; nobody enjoys a tongue that takes over.

Breathing, pauses and eyes

A few small details make a big difference once you are past the first kiss. Breathe through your nose so you do not have to break away every few seconds. Close your eyes most of the time; it helps you focus on how the kiss feels and keeps things from getting awkward. Short pauses are not a failure either. Pulling back an inch, resting your foreheads together and then leaning back in can feel even more intimate than kissing nonstop.

Reading their response

Good kissers adjust as they go. If your partner presses closer, matches your pace or makes happy little sounds, you are on the right track. If they slow down, pull their head back slightly or kiss you more softly, follow that cue and ease up. Kissing styles vary a lot from person to person, so what worked with someone else may not be what this person enjoys. Treat each new partner as someone to learn, not someone to perform for.

Where to put your hands

Hands can make a kiss feel more intimate, or awkward if they just hang there. Comfortable options include:

  • Gently cupping their face or jaw.
  • Resting a hand on the back of their neck or in their hair.
  • Holding their waist or lower back.
  • Lightly running your fingers along their arm.

Keep touch respectful and pay attention to how they respond. Moving your hands somewhere new is a natural moment to check in. Even a sweet kiss on the forehead or a long hug can be part of the moment.

Keep things interesting

Once you are comfortable, a little variety keeps make-outs from feeling routine:

  • Change the pace. Alternate slow, lingering kisses with a few quicker ones, then slow down again.
  • Kiss beyond the lips. Cheeks, jawline, forehead, neck and earlobes, if they enjoy it.
  • Use a light nibble. A gentle lip bite can be playful. Keep it soft, and skip it if they do not respond well.
  • Pause and smile. Pulling back for a second, making eye contact and smiling builds tension and connection.
  • Whisper something. A compliment or a soft “I've wanted to do that all night” adds intimacy. Our list of romantic things to say has ideas.

Try something new together

In a longer relationship, trying new things keeps the spark alive. Talk about it outside the moment: what you both like, what you would like more of and anything that is off-limits. Then experiment together:

  • Take turns being the one who leads the whole make-out.
  • Kiss for a minute without using your hands at all.
  • Slow everything down for an extra-long, unhurried session.
  • Change positions: standing against a wall, sitting face to face, lying side by side.

New does not have to mean wild. Small changes in pace, position or setting are enough to make it feel fresh.

Make out in different places, respectfully

Changing the setting can make a make-out feel memorable. Some ideas that stay private and considerate:

  • On a blanket under the stars in your backyard or on a balcony.
  • In front of a fireplace or under a pile of blankets during a movie night.
  • At the top of a scenic hike when nobody else is around.
  • In the kitchen while dinner is cooking.
  • A goodbye kiss at the door that turns into something longer.

Keep it age-appropriate for your surroundings, respect other people's spaces and follow the rules of public places. A quick kiss in public is sweet; a full make-out in front of strangers usually is not.

Build your confidence

Confidence makes kissing feel better for both people, and it grows with practice and a little self-kindness.

  • Remember they're probably nervous too. Most people worry about the same things you do.
  • Laugh off the awkward bits. Bumped noses and clinking teeth happen to everyone. Laughing together turns a stumble into a moment.
  • Focus on them, not on your performance. Paying attention to their responses takes you out of your head.
  • Ask for feedback. “What do you like?” is a confident question, and the answer makes you a better kisser for them specifically.
Tip: If you notice they are pulling back, stiffening or giving short responses, slow down or stop and check in. Reading signals and respecting them is the most attractive skill a kisser can have.

It also helps to talk about kissing outside the moment. Telling a partner “I loved it when you did that” the next day reinforces what works and makes it easier for them to share what they like, too. Over time, those small conversations turn two good kissers into a great pair.

Common make-out mistakes to avoid

  • Going too fast or too deep right away.
  • Using too much tongue or too much saliva.
  • Keeping your eyes wide open the whole time.
  • Ignoring signals that they want to slow down or stop.
  • Assuming kissing means they want to go further.

The bottom line

The best tips to make out come down to a few simple things: get a clear yes, start slow, pay attention, mix it up and keep it fun. When both of you feel comfortable and wanted, the technique tends to take care of itself.
takeaways: Consent is ongoing: look for clear signals and check in, especially when things change.
Start slow with soft, relaxed kisses and ease into deeper kissing together.
Vary the pace, add kisses beyond the lips and try new settings to keep it fresh.
Confidence comes from focusing on your partner and laughing off awkward moments.

faq.q: How do you make out for the first time?
faq.a: Make sure you both want to, start with soft closed-mouth kisses, tilt your head slightly and relax your lips. Follow your partner's pace and ease into deeper kissing only if you are both enjoying it. Fresh breath and a comfortable, private spot help you both relax.

faq.q: How do you know if someone wants to make out?
faq.a: Signs include lingering eye contact, glancing at your lips, leaning closer, touching you and staying close. The clearest way to know is to ask, for example “Can I kiss you?” If they hesitate or pull away, respect it and give them space.

faq.q: What should I do with my hands while making out?
faq.a: Gently cup their face, rest a hand on the back of their neck, hold their waist or lower back or run your fingers along their arm. Keep touch respectful and pay attention to how they respond, checking in before moving your hands somewhere new.

faq.q: How long should a make-out session last?
faq.a: There is no right length. Some last a minute, others much longer. Let it last as long as you both enjoy it, and feel free to pause, talk or laugh in between. Stopping when either person wants to is always fine.
